line: I yell, ”Thanks for makin’ us in your image You got a good sense of hubris”

meaning:
A reference to Genesis 1:27 in which God says:

So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them.

While Chance is metaphorically on God’s shoulders, he thanks him for making humans have similarities and characteristics to God. However humans aren’t perfect like God after all.

The second part is a play on the phrase “you have a good sense of humor” except for Chance replaces humor with hubris. Hubris is a Greek term to describe a character who has become so prideful over their traits that they begin to believe they are godlike. God has a “good sense of hubris” because he created humans in his own image, because of this some of us tend to become hubristic and believe that we are godlike. However it is true that we are in fact “like God” since we were modeled after his image!

But when God designed humans in his image, he intended for us to NOT be hubristic. Instead he designed us to be the opposite, another philosophical term named Sophrosyne. Sophrosyne is the complete opposite of hubris, it means self control, humbleness, and balance. If he intended this in his design then it would mean he is very conscious of hubris, and would not want his children to become hubristic but rather humble creatures.

meaning:
After he’s had his fill with the splendors of fame, Chance took the time to recenter his focus and prioritize the things he deemed truly important: his family and his home.

Chicago was in very bad shape, with high crime rates and poverty-stricken residents. However, this was still the city Chance called home, and as such, he decided to do everything in his power to clean it up.

Just as an example of things that need to be changed in Chicago, Chance mentions “going in prisons and opening gates” and “cracking the code and opening safes” (paraphrasing). Chicago has an extremely high crime rate, due to the lack of proper education and other necessities. A lot of the “criminals” are almost forced into a life of crime due to their environment, and Chance plans on reforming this unjust situation and giving the people of Chicago a better chance at life. He also plans on “opening the safe”, a metaphor for obtaining a fortune that was once hidden away from the people. Chance wishes to take back their fortune from the state leaders and give the people the funding they deserve.



Chicago’s unfortunate circumstance is due to its leaders refusing to rightfully provide for its people. The less they give to their people, the more they keep for themselves. Hence, “the people were scattered, the leaders were flattered” (paraphrasing). However, no matter how much power these people feel they have, Chance will not stop until they are all rightfully removed.

Chance is well known in Chicago, his home, for much more than just his music. He has been a consistent provider and supporter of the city for as long as he’s been rapping: giving millions of dollars to Chicago’s education system, starting a non-profit organization to provide for those in need, and even earning BET’s Humanitarian Award for his contributions to his communities.

For reasons greater than the people themselves, Chicago isn’t what you would call a “healthy home”, with its high crime and death rates, along with a lack of good educational facilities, and some other unfortunate circumstances.

But Chance has been working incredibly hard at reforming the city, giving much of his own money, time, and effort in the process. With his help, the city can finally develop into the wonderful home it was meant to be.

To summarize:
“My city a riot, I go on a diet” – Chicago is not in the best place when Chance isn’t there to help support it.
“But if I keep eating, they’ll have a parade” – As long as Chance continues his own individual growth, he will be able to provide more for his city.

line: Body the body, the body, the body, the body The body, the body, the head

meaning:
This repeated line is likely a Biblical reference that may be meant to reflect Chance’s position/responsibility within his community or the world as a whole. It refers to followers of Christ making up “the body of Christ” and Christ being considered “the head” of the church. This can be seen in 1st Corinthians 12:12-27 CSB and Ephesians 4:13-16 CSB and other scriptures throughout the Bible. With these scriptures in mind, it causes the listener to realize that they too are a part of “the body” and a part of “the problem” and have responsibility for their community as well, no matter how big or small.

The other lines around this repeated lyric refer to Moses parting the red sea and the children of Israel crossing the red sea, but complaining after they fled Egypt. Moses had a responsibility to his people as the leader or “the head”, but so did the children of Israel who at large did not meet their responsibilities or contribute in a positive manner to their community.

line: The sea get too choppy, the people get wocky And Israel’s salty the water is dead

meaning:
The Dead Sea is a lake that borders Jordan and Israel, named after the fact that the water is so salty that little to no aquatic life can live there.

When water is choppy, that means there are a bunch of small, unorganized waves. This makes it difficult to swim in and surf. So Chance here is alluding to waves, which can mean the newest trends, and by calling them choppy, he can be saying that there isn’t anything as impactful or inspiring about the new hip hop coming out, which would make “people wocky” or act weird/unusual.

Choppy waves can also refer to people losing relationships to loved ones and family. Chance was instrumental to the completion of Kanye West’s song Waves, which used waves to symbolize how your family and friends make you feel. He even had his own mix of the song, which Kanye opted out of using. So if your “waves get choppy,” that could mean you lost your connection to people who matter most to you. Consider the fact that this song was released after/in the midst of the coronavirus pandemic, which triggered lockdowns and social distancing, making many feel isolated and alone.

line: We not in Kansas, like Patrick Mahomes Over the rainbow and back in the two flat The witches is too flat, they shattered they bones The house is too heavy
vault_lines: We not in Kansas, like Patrick Mahomes
meaning:
The phrase “We’re not in Kansas anymore” is a reference to The Wizard of Oz after Dorothy is magically transported to the land of Oz she tells her dog, “Toto, I have a feeling we’re not in Kansas anymore”. The phrase refers to a fish out of water experience in which someone is in a new environment that feels foreign to them; this may be referring to Chance’s experiences after starting to gain fame and riches. This experience may also be shared by the quarterback for the Kansas City NFL Team, Patrick Mahomes, who like Chance had a promising talent in high school that has made him a star. After landing in Kansas City (ironically not in Kansas) Mahomes was able to lead his team to a Super Bowl win in 2019.



Somewhere Over the Rainbow is a song sung by the one of a kind talent Judy Garland in the film adaptation of The Wizard of Oz. In the film, Dorothy is transported to Oz in a tornado that figuratively takes her ‘over the rainbow’ to a dreamy place that she yearns for but soon finds out that while there is some whimsical charm to Oz there is also danger that she was unprepared to face. After conquering the Wicked Witch of the West, Dorothy is given a secret spell that will take her home. She must click the heels of the red ruby shoes she was given upon arrival in Oz and say, “there’s no place like home”. The movie ends with Dorothy having learned to appreciate the people in her life and returning home to Kansas to joyously reunite with her family and friends. Additionally, Chance comically points out that when Dorothy’s house lands in Oz it is ‘too heavy’ and it crushes the Witch of the East flattening her and crushing her to death.

https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/villains/images/7/72/Wicked_Witch_of_the_East_is_dead.jpg/revision/latest?cb=20110608234004

Perhaps though, Chance compares his struggles with his life-work balance and fame, with Dorothy’s character arc in the movie. Chance and Dorothy both had big dreams but realized soon after achieving them that they weren’t prioritizing the important things in their lives–their families. Chance reflected on his time as an acid riddled young up-and-comer in the game during his Acid Rap days and returned home to be with family as he recovered from his reliance on drugs. The opening lines of his verse may be referring to his relationship with his beloved wife, Kirsten Corley, when formerly they were an on-again off-again couple and co-parents. Chance also has ‘Savemoney back in his blood’ after numerous rumors of fallings out between him and his friends in the rap collective. Just like Dorothy, Chance had the ability to have all that he wanted the whole time, but had to realize what that was and as they say, “there’s no place like home”.

1And God spake all these words, saying, 2I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. 3Thou shalt have no other gods before me. 4Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth.

Many civilizations in the old Testament built statues out of stone to signify a god that the people would worship, such as the god of the sea, or the god of fertility. Chance here is pointing out that civilizations today have done the same thing with modern replacements, creating gods out of money, fame, or even other people. meaning: At first, you start coming to church and you finally decide one day I’m going to clap. I’m not going to clap louder than everybody else, but I just felt that. Then, the next thing you get is you start to get that one hand up. Then, you get a little more confidence. The next time you come you got two hands up. Then, you’re standing up, and you start to realize as you’re rapping that that looks like Wu-Tang. Wu-Tang.

line: We give the glory to You, God One livin’ true God, You make us booyah
vault_lines: We give the glory to You, God
meaning: So first of all, you know, the reason why we got married beyond locking in our family and tradition and love and all those things, it is a part of I believe what were are supposed to do. Everything wasn’t fulfilled just because I made a Christian rap album, you know what I mean? There’s certain things that you got to do to be right, or to be at peace. So, we give the glory to him first of all for even allowing this to happen or giving us the strength to make it to there. Then, we just got to let him know who he talking to. The one living true God, they called them Yahweh back in the day, the God of Israelites.

line: [Verse 3]
vault_lines: My baby mama went celibate
meaning: I would say the third verse was written probably six months after I started working on the first and second verse, and so a lot changed. I was engaged by that point. Me and my wife together conquered my cigarette addiction, so I went on a little sabbatical with her and came back and was cigarette free. We got pregnant. That was like a big deal. That was a big change I feel like is us about to have another kid. I think everybody has eras. Even if you’re not Kanye West where you can categorize it by what clothes he’s wearing, what the bear look like on different albums, like everybody in the world goes through different little eras and moments in their life.

line: It’s two different things It’s too bad, and it’s so sad It’s too bad, and it’s so sad
vault_lines: It's two different things
meaning: My mom used to always say when I was ask for too much, she’d say, “Too bad, so sad.” That’s a common saying. I feel like we’ve all heard too bad, so sad before. And I think like I said, I wrote this song in pieces. I would say the first two parts were the closest in time, but they were both very much so on the side of trying to figure it out, trying to get to a certain point that was right. Then, when I got to this part of the end of the song, it was like it is too bad, and it’s so sad. It’s too bad because shit, I need my family together, and it’s so sad because it doesn’t seem like it’s going to work out the way that it was supposed to.

line: They don’t take teenage angst at no banks
vault_lines: They don't take teenage angst at no banks
meaning: If they took teenage angst at banks, man, I would be a super rich man, because I felt it, but also I think it’s also like on a certain level about your output. So, separate from my own personal life that I put out on the record all the time, a lot of people connect it with Acid Rap on a certain level because it was such a lost and rebellious project. There’s so many questions being asked. There’s so much uncertainty. The difference between that and Coloring Book and The Big Day is that it’s a lot of exclamations. It’s a lot of, “This is what I’m on. This is what I believe. This is what I’m going to do.” And that teenage angst kind of got removed a little bit over time with me getting more and more things as I needed them to be, getting them all in place. So, I think that part was me telling myself, “You can’t just keep writing about what’s wrong all the time or what you’re trying to find or what you’re trying to search.” That shit is not accepted at no banks, yo. That shit is in the air. And try some new hues like Langston going to paint. Oh my God. Who is this dude writing this stuff? Try some new hues like Langston trying to paint? I can’t even break it down for you. If you don’t know about the Harlem renaissance, do your research.

line: Who the fuck rocked the boat? It’s gon’ sank Shootin’ at me point blank with those blanks
vault_lines: Who the fuck rocked the boat? It's gon' sank
meaning: I think like the shooting at me point blank with those blanks and trying to rock the boat, those are all references to that change, like when I felt the real difference in the relationship when my wife took sex out of the relationship. Not to mention I’m still out here doing whatever. I was in a position where I felt like my security was getting messed with, like my feeling to be able to do whatever I want and feeling proud and boastful about what was going on was getting changed.  I feel like shooting at me point blank with those blanks on one level is just me still being mad at DeVon Franklin, but it’s also me kind of expressing that shit wasn’t working right, you know what I mean? I couldn’t have a kid when she was celibate or even before that, because I don’t think we was ready for it. Wasn’t living right. I wasn’t living right, sorry.

line: Got me pressed, tryin’ to find DeVon Frank
vault_lines: Got me pressed, tryin' to find DeVon Frank
meaning: DeVon Franklin is an author and public speaker and just cool dude. I never met him before, but there was a time when I hated DeVon Franklin’s guts. I hated that nigga, for real, for real, because DeVon Franklin married Megan Good. When him and Megan Good got married, it became a partner group that would go out and do these motivational speeches. They eventually wrote a book together. This book was called The Wait. I remember the day that The Wait found itself into my home. The Wait is a book that’s written about how celibacy and taking sex out of your relationship or pre-marital sex out of your relationship can overall strengthen it and create an eternal thing. I was so fucking mad when I saw The Wait at my house dude, when I saw my girl reading this book. I’m looking at this nigga’s smile on the front and he’s with Megan Good. I’m like, “Yo, who is this nigga trying to ruin my shit?” And so, there was a point where I was pressed trying to find DeVon Frank. I feel like, once again, I don’t preach to anybody that celibacy is the way for them or anything like that, but even post already having a kid, post living together after being in it for so long, celibacy saved my life and gave me a marriage. So, now it’s shout out DeVon Frank, but at the time it was like where is DeVon Franklin at, yo? I got to come see this nigga.

line: Tried to try that with my girl, she “No thanks” Dropped the bomb, I couldn’t find a Tom Hanks
vault_lines: Tried to try that with my girl, she "No thanks"
meaning: I’ve known my wife since I was nine, yo. So, my wife is not impressed by a lot of the things that other people can be impressed by. I have all these things, all these accolades, and it was like that’s not what was keeping her there, you know? My faithfulness, my attention, my dedication are the things that she was looking for. With those absent, fuck is she staying around for? And “Dropped the bomb, I couldn’t find a Tom Hanks,” that’s based on a great nostalgic movie for a lot of people called ‘Forest Gump’ where Tom Hanks tells a story of his whole life and how he impacted all these different things through just being himself and not even fully knowing how impactful he was. There’s a scene where he goes to war and there’s a big bombing, and he goes and he picks up everybody on his back and he takes them out of the jungle. So, he picks up lieutenant Dan, but he’s looking for Bubba. Bubba’s his best friend, and he’s trying to protect Bubba while all these bombs are dropping. So, he goes and he grabs lieutenant Dan. And he goes back out into the jungle to find Bubba, but there’s another dude’s leg got blown off that he needs to help. Then, he comes back to find Buba, and there’s another dude. He keeps making all these trips on his way to Bubba, but helping everybody else. Then, finally when he gets to Bubba it’s too late, and he’s dying. I thought that was a great explanation of how I have put so many things ahead of it trying to save everybody except for my best friend.

line: Fuck bein’ one of the G.O.A.T.s, I’m Gotenks
vault_lines: Fuck bein’ one of the G.O.A.T.s, I'm Gotenks
meaning: So DBZ reference real quick, you know what I’m saying, for my manga fans. Yeah, so Gotenks is Goten and Trunks when they would do the dance, and they become one. It was just another me trying to say how dope I am. I don’t know. I’m more than one. I don’t know. Everybody else wants to be the G.O.A.T. that’s the thing is like, “Oh, he’s a G.O.A.T. he’s one of the G.O.A.T.S. I don’t know. I always hated that term, G.O.A.T.S.

line: So much style, my stylist got no dresser Fuck goin’ straight to the pros, I’m professor
vault_lines: So much style, my stylist got no dresser
meaning: So I was feeling myself at the time, you know what I’m saying? You know, things are going well for me, you know? And so much style my stylist got no dresser, you know, like she not pulling clothes from nowhere. This is my steed.

line: Three damn Grammys, my Granny like, “No pressure”
vault_lines: Three damn Grammys, my Granny like, "No pressure"
meaning:
My grandma always put pressure on me. I’ve always been in her prayers, and she’s always wanted me to be successful and to talk about God in my music. So, she could see me talking about God in my music, but I wasn’t having these hard conversations with my grandmother about how I was acting towards my wife or why we were breaking up. Obviously, she’s getting at, “You got it, baby. Go ahead. Blah, blah, blah.” You know, like I knew because of how real our relationship was growing up that I wasn’t doing exactly what she wanted me to do.
There’s so many different areas in our lives that we have to do things for ourselves, you know what I mean? The Grammy’s were great, and that was great for myself, for the music, for independence, for all these things, but what does it mean for my household if my wife’s not there, or what does it mean for my child if she’s waking up and she doesn’t know where her dad is yet until I get on the phone with her? It wasn’t the best thing for me, but people were giving me that, “No pressure, you got this. You’re doing everything right.”

line: My wife nanny like Fran Drescher
vault_lines: My wife nanny like Fran Drescher
meaning: So, my wife, and I’m sure a lot of people’s wife, she wasn’t my wife at the time, but a lot of people’s women if you have kids, they hold down the fort for you. They not only provide you with the ease and the comfort and the solace or place to come and grieve or get whatever support you need, but also they do that for your children. Like I was just saying, the single dad, mingle dads, that shit is hard, yo. So, having my wife be available in the capacity that she was for myself and for my kid, it was like she was like the nanny, but it’s like that’s why the Fran Drescher line is kind of cool, because eventually he marries the nanny. We know how that story goes.

line: But he go high
vault_lines: But he go high
meaning: This hook feels like it’s like an inception. It’s so funny. So many articles that wrote about this song, first of all, because this video wasn’t made they don’t understand all the references in the lyrics, but the thing that stands out to everybody is when they go low, we go high. But when I wrote the song I wasn’t thinking about the first lady, Michele Obama. Shout out to them, though. You guys did a great job. I wasn’t thinking about that line. I think the we go high was just how I came out of the verse. It just felt right, and I didn’t really put it in context of today’s politics or understanding the gravity of Michele Obama being a black woman who was successful in her own right running a law firm and everything. Then, she came together with Barack and made him what he is. I didn’t have all that understanding and context back then. Then, when people heard it back and they’re like, “He got that from Michele Obama.” I’m like, “Damn, I did. That’s crazy.”

line: [Verse 2]
vault_lines: My baby mama went celibate
meaning: I think the best part of this song is that fundamentally as a narrative, it doesn’t really work. It gives you an impossible situation, right? It gives you the conflict or the issue up front, right? Then the second verse talks about when I was by myself experiencing all of these gifts and blessings and things that were coming into me that made me feel like I should be whole, but I still wasn’t. So it’s two versus of conflict, and then the third verse kind of never really tells you how I got to that point. It’s just like, we’ve reached the finish line. And I think the best part about it is that it doesn’t really make sense. It wasn’t just like I had the realization, yes, it’s good and then Kirsten, or maybe it is that, but there’s not like anything beyond a divine reasoning why it worked out.

line: I mean, I ain’t gon’ promise that the pain go away And you can take your sweet time, but she ain’t gon’ wait ’Cause a new coat of paint don’t make the stain go away
vault_lines: I mean, I ain't gon' promise that the pain go away
meaning: When my girl left me, I didn’t really have a choice in anything. You know what I mean? Like it wasn’t like I could convince her anything different, and I was also trying to convince myself that that was the route that I was supposed to be taking. Most rappers don’t get married at that young, or ever have a kid with somebody and then later marry them. Like they usually, if they’re good dads, they figure that out and they also like move on and figure it out later themselves. And so I had a lot of times where I was convincing myself that it was nothing I could do to repair it. And you know, “A new coat of paint don’t make the stain go away,” is kind of like a point when I was convincing myself like, you could do all that. Like you know, getting saved, and practicing celibacy on your own, separate from your girl. Like, it was just like, “She’s going to do her thing, she left you, it’s over. You know what I’m saying? And all this stuff that you’re trying to do to purify yourself is for naught, so quit it.” And all that was to say like, “Shut up, self.” Like, he go high.

line: I just want the shine back like a Eagles fan My ego like, ”Ah damn, there he go Prayin’ again, again, the same ol’ thang”
vault_lines: I just want the shine back like a Eagles fan
meaning: Shout out DeSean Jackson, shout out the Eagles. They got my boy back. So first of all, got to throw out a little wordplay. But also it was, in essence, it’s just about the duality of self. Like when you pray, when you pray for real, you got to get on your knees. You got to say that stuff out loud. You got to take time to yourself. Like, there’s always prayer before breakfast and dinner and “Oh yeah, I’m a pray for you,” that kind of stuff. But when you feel it, and you’re at your lowest and you really go out and you really in a room speaking in an empty room, and you feel like that’s the only way that’s going to get you out of there, there’s still always going to be a part on the inside of yourself that’s doubting.  And so I had to deal with my mind being like, “Oh you going to pray over this too?” Like, “This is your go-to when things get hard?” And I’m glad that that voice didn’t overpower how I felt.

line: Big hands for my ring, I’ma need a Pringles can
vault_lines: Big hands for my ring, I'ma need a Pringles can
meaning: I got a big ass hand. My hands have been the same size since I was like seven years old. They’d used to drag behind me. So that’s just been a thing. But it’s also like, I think it was to really illustrate when men think about getting married, they think about really getting locked down. I think even more so than women do. They think about the end of something, rather than the beginning of something. And I think at that time I was just like, “I need like five or six years to like figure things out and then we’ll get married.” Like, that’s how I would talk about it to her. And I think I just had this mindset that it was like, “Because my life is big because I feel like I’m larger than life, it’s going to take a lot to lock me down,” and it’s not a Pringles can, but there is a lot of Vivi’s in there. They’re doing a big dance right now. It’s a little joint on there.

line: You could fall much faster than you think you can
vault_lines: You could fall much faster than you think you can
meaning: That’s about the fall from grace. It’s about that feeling of like, you become a giant, but the bigger you get, the faster you fall. And I was in a position where I had built up all this feeling around me of like fixing everything and being perfect, and I was living in probably the most imperfect space that I had ever occupied.

line: I tried to do the single-dad mingle-dance
vault_lines: I tried to do the single-dad mingle-dance
meaning: So, me and my wife split, and I started doing my thing, you know what I’m saying? I didn’t have like a pressing album to come out or anything. I just won all the Grammy’s. I’m thinking it’s cool. And so I just started going out every night, literally every night. Even before we found like separate homes, like I was staying at a hotel, I had a penthouse at the Waldorf, and you know, I was doing my thing.  And the single-dad mingle-dance is probably one of the most uncomfortable awkward dance as possible. You’re supposed to be representing all these things. There’s also all these virtues and stuff, but I’m out being scandalous. That’s probably the best word.

line: Tired of the rumors, every room had an elephant Tryna find her shoes, rummagin’ through the skeletons
vault_lines: Tired of the rumors, every room had an elephant
meaning: I feel like when we were initially together right after the baby came, I wasn’t living right. Like you get to a certain degree of success, and you start to believe that all these different things are owed to you. So I wasn’t faithful. I wasn’t kind. I wasn’t understanding. I wasn’t helpful in a lot of ways. I just wasn’t all the way there. And so when I talk about every room had an elephant, it’s saying not even just on the sex side, but just like every level of the relationship, there’s an elephant in the room that’s not being addressed. That’s where that saying comes from. That we got to address the elephant in the room, because it’s like we’re sitting here acting like nothing’s going wrong. And then I go on to say, “Trying to find her shoes, rummagin' through the skeletons.” It’s like there’s so many skeletons in my closet that it’s like she can’t do a regular everyday thing without coming across something that I did wrong, something that I’m trying to hide, and yeah, she took away sex. Took me out of my element. I didn’t know how to act after that.

line: BeBe & CeCe, I need like 20 twins
vault_lines: BeBe & CeCe, I need like 20 twins
meaning:
Chance references BeBe and CeCe Winans, a brother and sister with a two-year age difference who were both members of the sizable Winans musical family and collaborated as BeBe & CeCe Winans on the number-one R&B single “Addictive Love” in 1991.



Similarly, Chance and his younger brother Taylor Bennett have each succeeded in their own right and have collaborated on tracks such as “Broad Shoulders” and “Grown Up Fairy Tales”. While they are the only two Bennett siblings, he wishes he could have as expansive of a musical family as the Winans.

Considering his reference to Proud Family protagonist Penny in the previous line, he may be referencing characters BeBe and CeCe Proud (both voiced by Tara Strong), twins who are named after the singers.

line: My baby mama went celibate Lies on my breath, she say she couldn’t take the smell of it

The term “celibate” typically means that someone is abstaining from marriage and sexual interactions due to religious obligations. However, based on this verse it seems that his baby mama is abstaining from sexual relations due to Chance’s lies and potential alcohol consumption.

On his 2016 mixtape Coloring Book, Chance states that he has turned his baby mama into his fiancée.

Originally known as Saul of Tarsus, Paul persecuted early followers of Jesus until he was converted by God. God appeared to Saul as a “beam of light” and blinded him for 3 days. “Holy War” is viewed as a conflict between religions; however, among people of faith it’s more commonly used to describe the struggle between one’s faith in God and the temptation of this world.

When The-Dream talks about being safe, he doesn’t mean being protected against his enemies, he means to be protected against himself. He wants to stop the inner bickering between what’s right and what’s wrong and try to not be controlled by his egotistical self.

In short, he is looking to find his inner peace.

As the intro of “Jesus Walks” says:

Between lines “Somewhere I can feel safe” and “And end my holy war” you can hear a sample from Counter-Strike, precisely the line ““throwin' flashbang!””. It’s pretty quiet in song, but it’s definitely sampled.

“But I’m Looking for more” refers to the inherently insubstantial nature of religious faith. Faith is not rooted in facts or reasoning, but only in spiritual feeling.

Kanye had previously established a metaphor of Faith as an “Ultra-light beam". Here he further develops that metaphor. The ultralight beam, is insubstantial – it’s light can be seen and it’s warmth can be felt but it has no physical substance.

meaning:
Rumored to be the title of Kanye’s next album ever since Graduation dropped, “good ass job” is also something of a meme phrase in Chance’s lexicon.

As of the release of “Ultralight Beam,” he was working on his third mixtape, the follow up to 10 Day and Acid Rap. Chance releases all his music for free to reach the widest audience possible. However, this release strategy would have made him ineligible for a Grammy, which previously only accepted commercially released albums.

On June 6th, 2016—almost a month after the release of Chance’s Coloring Book—the Recording Academy released a press statement to announce that streaming-only albums would now be eligible for Grammy nomination. The change was likely inspired by a petition started by Chance after receiving encouragement from Pharrell Williams.

At the 2017 Grammys, Chance would indeed snatch the awards for Best New Artist, Best Rap Performance for “No Problem”, and Best Rap Album for Coloring Book, which became the first stream-only album to ever win a Grammy.

As it happens, just a few days after it was released, fans did in fact tweet every single one of Chance’s lyrics off Coloring Book.

Furthermore, on September 17, 2018 at one of Chance’s Open Mic Nights in Chicago, Kanye announced that the two were working on a collab album titled, Good Ass Job.

vault_lines: There's gonna be frustration in this white man's game
meaning:
Here, Chance (quoting his mother) plays on the double meaning of “tied up.” On one level, it refers to being caught and punished by the system—arrested or otherwise entangled in legal trouble. Even with marijuana being legalized, she warns that the same white-controlled institutions (politicians, police, lawmakers) will still find ways to keep Black people trapped in the “game.”

There’s also a darker metaphor: “tied up” recalls the history of Black people being physically restrained or lynched by white oppressors. Calling weed a “tree” reinforces this layered wordplay—linking marijuana to both the literal plant and to the trees where such violence historically took place.

line: Before they build another golf course, library Or send a eminent domain to Miss Mary

meaning:
This is a conversation about gentrification, a process of building luxury locations but then forcing old citizens out of those areas. This can be done privately to build golf courses, or this can be done publicly with libraries. “Eminent domain” is when the government forces the sale of homes from citizens to build new areas. These new areas make the places richer, but then the market value of houses surrounding the location are increased, leading to those residents now unable to afford those locations. Poor residents living in impoverished areas need cheap housing, but when that area gets improved, the housing is no longer cheap and those citizens that were supposed to be helped get displaced.

“We want to make sure when it floats, we float with it.”

line: We need CBA, CBA, CBA Barry

CBA stands for Community Benefits Agreement, which is an agreement made by tenants of an area to ensure that nobody in that area gets displaced. It is a response to gentrification that pushes long time residents out of the city they can no longer afford.

“Barry” is short for Barack Obama, who was deeply interested in displacement, and yet a library in his name displaced citizens of Chicago.

http://www.obamacba.org/

CBA is also notably a way for workers to unite against their employer for bargaining. This unites the themes of family sticking together to workers sticking together to increase pay so “then everybody get rich”.

Conjoined twins, also commonly known as Siamese twins, are two babies who are born physically connected to each other – thus causing them to be twins. When Chance says he’s trying to “Siamese ‘em”, he’s saying that he wants his heart and mind to be like Siamese twins – deeply connected.

Furthermore, Chance seems to suggest that the head and heart are at war (“they always going head to head”) and that he is trying to get them to be in sync, much like Siamese twins, who often need to be deeply in sync with one another to function. It’s also possible chance is punning on “head to head”–many Siamese twins are joined at the head–instead of butting heads, he wants them to be connected there.

In Greek mythology, King Midas had the ability to turn anything he touched into gold. This ability is known as the Midas touch.

In Christianity, many count the Devil’s ability to make promises that seem extremely appealing as one of the Devil’s greatest strengths. Chance poetically says that the Devil has the ability to make lies “golden” by making them much more desirable than the truth–the lies he tell seem appealing, and the false promises he makes seem golden.

Raury illustrates this sentiment in his song Devil’s Whisper:

I can give you everything
Diamonds
Everything you touch can be
Golden
But first you gotta listen to me

Throughout the song, Chance argues that those trying to find the truth will not have to fight against those who suppress it, but also against the Devil distracting them with an alternate truth that will appear to be much better than what was originally sought after.

Those that’ll tell don’t know and those that know won’t tell

Then, the character Mookie steps up and affirms that Mayor does not know anything. A possible interpretation of this line is that it is an admonition to not snitch, or speak to authority. They were part of a crew called Save Money, now best known as a launch pad for rappers. At the time, though, it was a motley collection of teenage boys from the city’s selective-enrollment schools who would chill downtown and do, in Chance’s words, ‘illegal, fucked-up shit’: jumping CTA turnstiles, smoking weed, and getting into fights, mostly.

meaning:
Firstly, there’s a possible double entendre on the work “acid” since it can refer to his most famous and acclaimed project, Acid Rap (2013). After The Big Day (2019) and Chance’s six-year absence, online discourse theorized that Chance the Rapper should take acid again to achieve the same lyrical, creative, and career highs as that era.

Chance is stating that if listeners want him to try acid again, they should do it themselves, pushing back at the notion that he needs drugs to create great music. The lines touch on a classic debate on rap and art in general that is the use of drugs to produce or enhance creative drive. Aldous Huxley’s The Doors of Perception (1954) is a common citation as it  argues for psychedelics as a genuine perceptual and creative tool — a direct contrast to what Chance is saying here. The lines reject the psychedelic-as-fuel arguments and afirms emotional authenticity to the real engine of art (“love was the fuel and the pen was the tool”).

Notably Chance likely also feels a sort of missionary component to his music since he is preaching the gospel  (celebration of the good news)of Christ in many of his songs. Christians believe that it is there mission to spread the word about Jesus and what better way to do it than touring as an immensely popular artist. line: I took the throne on distant shores
vault_lines: I took the throne on distant shores
meaning:
As contributor Catapan noted, the previous line references The Emperor Jones, the play by African-American playwright Eugene O'Neil–this line continues that reference. As Catapan noted: “After killing another black man during a dice game, [Brutus Jones] is imprisoned but later escapes to a remote, undeveloped Caribbean island, where he crowns himself emperor.” Brutus escaped from America to a distant shore, the Caribbean Islands, where he took the throne by crowning himself emperor. The play is largely Jones recounting his journey of running through the jungle from former subjects who have rebelled against him. Perhaps Chance feels as though he has been on the run from former fans who have rebelled against him after he released The Big Day.

Beyond this, however, one can also read this as continuing the extended metaphor of The Odyssey. Odysseus was offered to marry multiple women, such as Calypso and Nausicaa. Calypso wants him as his husband, and Nausicaa’s father, a king, want him to take his daughter’s hand. However, Odysseus' loyalty to his wife on Ithaca prevented him. Now that Chance is separated from his wife, it allows the possibility of an alternative life.

Alternatively, Chance could be referring here to how Odysseus “took the throne” of Troy by winning the Trojan War. For Chance, this would be having global fame and recognition for his music.

line: I went to war, some Emperor Jones
vault_lines: I went to war, some Emperor Jones
meaning:
The Emperor Jones is a 1920 tragedy by American playwright Eugene O’Neill. It follows Brutus Jones, a clever and confident African American who once worked as a Pullman porter. After killing another black man during a dice game, he is imprisoned but later escapes to a remote, undeveloped Caribbean island, where he crowns himself emperor.

The play is notable for its innovative use of expressionism and symbolism – most of the action follows Jones alone as he flees through the jungle, pursued by the island’s inhabitants, while the relentless beat of a tom-tom drum grows faster, mirroring his mounting fear. Through a series of hallucinatory episodes, Jones confronts visions of slavery, chain gangs, and his own past crimes, blending personal guilt with a broader historical reckoning.

When it premiered with the Provincetown Players, it marked a milestone in American theatre by offering a complex, high-profile role for a Black actor.

As Jeremih continues on from his intro, the essence and message of the song is highlighted, as he alludes to the fact that he wants to spend time with his loved one, especially at Christmas. This also coincides with the title of the song, ‘snowed in’.

The idea of staying inside and being with her is further shown, other than the title, through his lyricism. He implies this through them not needing to go to the club to enjoy themselves, as they have this relationship together.

Getting ‘snowed in’ is often seen as a negative experience, however in the song, both Chance and Jeremih uses it in a positive way, as they can spend more time with their loved ones. The two-way motif that it represents comes in a physical sense, as they are snowed in from the “white Christmas at the crib”, as well as an emotional resonance for both of them, as it serves as a way for them to get closer.

Jeremih in the hook, and Chance later on in the song, speak of their newfound ‘maturity’, as they move away from one night stands and absence of admiration and commitment, again shown through Jeremih not going to the club. This development is to more emotional attachment and intimacy, which a relationship often offers.

line: World on my back like leech (Ch-ch), mafia fam like Meech (Ch-ch)
vault_lines: World on my back like leech (Ch-ch), mafia fam like Meech (Ch-ch)
meaning:
This is in reference to 2 people:

The first reference is to Philadelphia rapper Meek Mill who made the headlines in 2018 after a Philadelphia judge sentenced him to two to four years in prison last year for a series of probation violations following his 2008 conviction for drug and weapons charges.
Many people, activists, and celebrities were in shock by the judge’s decision to put Meek Mill behind bars for a minor crime.
After several months behind bars, his months-long legal battle, which included star-studded endorsements and a #FreeMeekMill social media campaign, turned turned the 30-year-old into a symbol of what activists say is systemic racism and abuse in the criminal justice system, in the U.S. in general and in Philadelphia in particular.
After several months behind bars, Meek was released from prison after the Pennsylvania Supreme Court ordered a judge to free him on bail and headed straight to a Philadelphia 76'rs  playoff game.

The second reference is to Big Meech, co-leader of the notorious The Black Mafia Family (BMF).
A drug trafficking organization originally based in Detroit, Michigan which was founded in the late 1980s by brothers Terry and Demetrius “Big Meech” Flenory. The organization had a precne in Hip Hop with their entertainment company, BMF Entertainment. It’s alleged that the label helped promote the careers of rappers Fabolous and Jeezy.

In September 2008, Meech and his brother were sentenced to 30 years in prison for running a nationwide cocaine-trafficking ring, which lasted from 2000 to 2005 after a federal investigation .

The use of Wendy in this verse acts as a reference to the story of Peter Pan.

The window and shadow play an important role in Peter Pan. The window is the connection between Peter Pan and Wendy’s worlds. When Peter returns for his shadow through the window, he awakes Wendy and they begin their adventure in Neverland.

At the end of the story, Wendy offers Peter the chance to live with her, but he declines as he does not want to become an adult.  The window is a metaphor for the connection between Chance and this girl, and when Chance says that he’s a shadow of his former self, he’s saying that he isn’t the same person he was back when he met her.



This shows how Chance was caught up in the past, hoping that things between him and this girl would never change, but he soon realized that she grew up and is not the same girl she once was anymore.

Chance and Joey Bada$$ also have a song named “Wendy and Becky”, which uses “Wendy” as a homophone for “Windy” to refer to the Windy City, Chicago, which is Chance The Rapper’s Hometown. Chance’s mentor, Kanye West has also referred to Chi-Town as Wendy in his single “Homecoming”.

line: But they got money for riot gear

meaning: Continuing on the statement in the previous line, the lack of PPE or personal protective equipment was a major problem for medical personnel during the COVID-19 pandemic. In addition, this period of time saw great civil unrest and resurgence in Black Lives Matter protests as well as calls to defund the police. Reportings throughout the year would often show law enforcement donning riot gear clashing with peaceful protesters, reinforcing why there was such a need to defund the police in the first place. Despite medical staff being forced to put themselves at risk by not being given adequate protective gear to treat patients, law enforcement seemed to have an abundance of resources and funding exemplified by their use of riot gear. This dichotomy is symbolic of the United States prioritizing punishment and destruction of its citizens' freedom over their well-being and survival. The United States showed its true colors when it covered its streets in red from the innocent and prioritized the lives of the blue and the white.

Mumia was closely aligned with the group MOVE, a Philly based group focused on racial injustice and environmentalism. Mumia had a long career of journalism and published writings before he was convicted. Mumia’s writings from death row have caused many protests and movements to end the death penalty. Julius Jones is a man on Death Row in Oklahoma. There is a large movement to free Julius Jones, due to a large amount of evidence that he is innocent. line: And hang us in a jail cell so they can swing the elections
vault_lines: And hang us in a jail cell so they can swing the elections
meaning: In the United States, the suicide rate inside prison is four times as high as in the general population. According to the US Census Bureau, the prison population is about 34% Black/African American while African Americans make up only about 12% of the US population. This is due to systemic racism, which encourages harsher sentences for crimes made by African Americans. It is also due to the “war on drugs” which was targeted solely at lower income communities of color, ignoring drug use in rich white communities. Much of this targeted racial injustice is designed to “swing the elections”, with many states revoking the right to vote from many prisoners. By reducing the African American voting population with targeted laws meant to grow the prison system, republican lawmakers increase their chance for re-election.

line: The manifested destiny a bunch of land they could steal

As the eastern coast of the United States became modernized and agrarian American Settlers expanded westward, coining the term “Manifest Destiny” to describe the feeling of entitlement and religious responsibility the settlers felt they had in modernizing the west. When expanding through the west, American settlers often had violent conflicts with Native American tribes, stealing their land, killing their livestock and destroying communities that had been on their land for centuries.

“The Rainbow Coalition’s ideology centered on class solidarity, uniting poor and working-class people across racial lines against shared oppression. Members of the Rainbow Coalition also sponsored a wide range of service programs at reduced or no costs to their respective communities, such as breakfasts for children, health clinics, bussing to prisons, daycare centers, clothing, ambulance services, among many other efforts.”

By referencing this in the context of lots of ghosts, Chance may be referring to other musicians &/or the music industry’s corruption at large. More broadly, he could be referring to followers of Jesus/God vs people who he thinks will not be saved & will therefore become “ghosts.”

In the context of the next line “get in the whip,“ Chance may be telling people this is their chance to stand together, avoid corruption, & get on board the ark, representing Christianity, now, before they turn to ghosts, meaning die or simply lose their way.

meaning:
When Chance returns home for the holidays, he is troubled by what he finds. He understands that he wields a large amount of power as a famous artist with a sizable following and that he is supposed to use this power to be a leader (he is supposed to be “the POTUS”), but he feels afraid that he cannot adequately fulfill the expectations he has built for himself (“the podium come up to my shoulders,” “I’m short and I’m shook and I’m broken”).

In Disney’s classic film The Lion King, the main character, Simba, experiences the death of his father at a very young age. Chance is drawing a parallel between his own anguish as a result of the troubles explained above and Simba’s anguish on Father’s Day.

line: Me and God playing tips ’cause he never gonna bounce on me, won’t bounce on me
vault_lines: Me and God playing tips 'cause he never gonna bounce on me, won't bounce on me
meaning:
Chance imagines him and God playing the basketball game “tips” and jokes that God will never leave his side.

In the basketball game Tips, players on one team attempt to make shots from the three-point line while the other team positions themselves around the basket.  If the shooter misses, the team around the goal can attempt to rebound and make the shot by jumping into the air and “tipping” the ball to one another, preventing it from hitting the ground and bouncing.

Chance uses this game as an analogy for how God will never bounce on him.

XXL: It’s interesting that he hasn’t released the production credits and as a nerd I’m mad at that, but it does lend this insular feeling of outsiders not knowing really who did the tracks.

Ivan: Right now it’s just a streaming only on Apple Music kind of thing, but I think as time goes on those production credits will be released. Like on “No Problem” alone I can list Jonathan Hoard, Rachel Cado, Jaime Woods, Baritone Williams and Cam O’bi as vocalists. That’s what made up that gospel choir.

XXL: Oh shit.

Ivan: Well, we made it sound like a sample by pitching up the vocals because that was the goal.

There’s also Jake Sherman, who played organ and James Frances who played piano. I also played a lot of organ and piano on it. We did a mixture of live drums and programmed drums. I will say the programmed drums in the mix are more prevalent, but there are certain live drums in there.

Even celebrities get caught wearing fake Yeezys, likely who Chainz is calling out, or, he’s calling out anyone who cops a fake pair instead of buying a real one. A quick google search shows you how easy it is to find fake Yeezys.

Considering his friendship with ‘Ye, Tity Boi wants everyone to support Kanye.

Fostering an unofficial relationship with True Religion Jeans has helped him amass a huge collection, so he’s not short of pockets. His net worth is $6 million, so he’s certainly not short of money.

That mind of ideas spawned his “Dabin' Sant” line of clothing, and during his Drink Champs Podcast appearance he revealed he’d made $2 million off this entrepreneurial spirit.

line: My woes up, I’m flippin’ those bucks, they doing toe tucks
vault_lines: My woes up, I'm flippin' those bucks, they doing toe tucks
meaning:
“Woe” is a term popularized by Drake on his track “Know Yourself.” The term is actually New Orleans slang for Whoadie, or people living in the same ward or area. All of Wayne’s family is doing well at present.

“Bucks” can refer to both money or livestock. It usually means to double your money from a drug sale, but the way Wayne has been releasing product and touring recently he’s pursuing more legal means.

A “toe tuck” is a move done in gymnastics when the gymnast literally tucks their toes while flipping.  The gymnast Wayne is referring to is “those bucks”, i.e. he is flipping his money.

Get pulled over for swervin’ like “Hi, officer,”

In 2015, he dropped the Free Weezy Album, and the hashtags #freethacarterv and #freec5 have popped up on social media, notably on the Twitter of Young Money overseer Mack Maine.

Despite the hashtags and the overt shots on Sorry 4 The Wait 2, Weezy was seen with Birdman during New Years 2016 for a Drake performance. In April of 2016 Birdman said himself on Hot ‘97’s “Ebro In The Morning” that the world deserves a Tha Carter V. But the album is nowhere to be seen.

https://youtu.be/K23_vkcsncA?t=26s

The meaning behind this is that you can not only knock the doors that are in your way down, but go as far as to present what’s holding the proverbial doors up to those who are trying to hold you back, so as to show them they can’t stop you.

This relates to Chance in that the music industry doesn’t want him to succeed as an independent artist, or that some people are against him making positive music for the people. Indeed, “they” don’t want him to win. Stay away from they.

Codeine is an opiate found in cough syrup.  The effects of the drug include drowsiness, which is why Wayne is moving so slowly, like a caterpillar.

Wayne’s famously a fan of sizzurp and has even been forced to give up the drink while on probation. In recent years he’s reaffirmed his love for the concoction, dedicating an entire song to it on Sorry 4 The Wait 2. Despite some believing he’d given the syrup up, he seems to say here it’s pretty obvious he’s back on the purple.



The second part of this lyric—“Fuck wrong with you? What you thinking? What you thought it was?“—is an echo of Chance’s verse on this track, bridging the situations of both rappers, showing how they aren’t even that different. Considering Lil Wayne’s issue with his label, this line and song about operative big labels is pretty powerful.

line: If one more label try to stop me It’s gon’ be some dreadhead niggas in ya lobby, huh huh
vault_lines: If one more label try to stop me
meaning:
Chance has always been open about his dislike for record labels, even going as far as personifying them as The Devil in some of his verses.

In an interview with HOT 97, Chance talked about why he doesn’t want to sign with a label, saying:

I have this understanding of it that could be changed at some point. But, I have complete control over my music, the same that I did when I was in high school: I make what I wanna make, when I wanna make it, with who I wanna make it with. And, in the end, I still own everything that I create. And just the understanding of giving up that piece of the pie to anybody, whether they’re a huge label, or a indie label, or it’s just a distribution deal or it’s just a publishing deal, like giving up that piece is difficult for me.

As Chano would later reveal in “Finish Line / Drown,” record labels are always trying to stop him from doing collaborations with other artists. Chance isn’t having it and is sending a warning to all the labels that are still trying to derail him and to the ones who haven’t tried yet. If they don’t stop messing with him, he’s going to send some people to their offices to make his message more clear.

Dreadlocks are a style associated with Chicago’s drill movement, and rappers like Waka Flocka and Chief Keef have helped popularize the hairstyle. It’s fitting that Chano included both 2 Chainz and Weezy in this song since the two have dreadlocks, making them “dreadheads.”



The line “There go Chano ridin' through the streets, they be like, "There he go!” is a reference to the hook on ScHoolboy Q’s “There He Go”:

I’m shining hard, they be like, “There he go!”
No bodyguard, they be like, “There he go!”
Up in your broad, they be like, “There he go!”
They be like, “There he go! Schoolboy, there he go!”

During “CoCo,” released in 2015 off his Sorry 4 The Wait 2 mixtape, Wayne rapped:

Who kept this shit together? N—, me, that’s who
Who was there when n—s left us? N—, me, that’s who

In the mid-2000s Jay Z attempted to sign Wayne to Rocafella, although the deal was just $175,000. Wayne showed his loyalty to Birdman by never entertaining any other contractual offers, despite all of the Hot Boyz leaving the label.

vault_lines: If one more label try to stop me

Like Chance, Wayne has issues with labels. But in Weezy’s case, it’s one label in particular: Cash Money.

In January 2015, Weezy sued Cash Money for $51 million in an effort to get out of his contract. One of the many issues Wayne raised in his lawsuit was that Birdman and Cash Money were preventing him from releasing his album, Tha Carter V.

In the performance of “No Problem” on The Ellen DeGeneres Show, Wayne replaced these lines with the following:

I'mma let ‘em rob me

Clearly poking fun at Olympic swimmer Ryan Lochte, who claimed that he and his crew had been robbed at gun point. They were later found to be lying, and Lochte admitted to having over-exaggerated what happened.

Spoiler Warning

  


Million Dollar Baby is a 2004 sports drama film co-starring Clint Eastwood (as Frankie Dunn), Morgan Freeman (as Eddie Dupris), and Hilary Swank (as Maggie Fitzgerald).

In the movie, Frankie is a professional boxer who owns a Los Angeles gym looked after by his best friend, ex-boxer Eddie “Scrap Iron” Dupris.

Maggie, a waitress from small-town Missouri, approaches Frankie to train her, but he’s reluctant to train a girl like her; however, when Frankie’s best fighter leaves, he agrees to train her.

After many months, Maggie proves to be an astounding fighter, knocking out opponents in round one. In any unlikely bond, as she fights across Europe, Frankie gives her the Gaelic name “Mo Chuisle,” a shortened form of “A, chuisle mo chroí” (English: ‘Oh, pulse of my heart’).

She returns to Las Vegas and, in a dirty fight, she gets paralyzed. They return to LA, and Maggie asks Frankie to help her to end her life—and he, with some reluctance, fulfills her wish, unplugging the respirator and inserting a fatal dose of adrenaline.



  


Maggie Fitzgerald, played by Hilary Swank, is the “million-dollar baby” who proved everyone wrong. She was a fighter like no other who had an unbreakable bond with her trainer.

Chance The Rapper is the father of two daughters—Kensli (b. Sep. 20, 2015) and Marli (b. Aug. 29, 2019). Thus, the line reads like a manifestation of the relationship he and his youngest daughter (two years old as of writing), Marli, will have.

line: I don’t want no autograph I just want a follow back, maybe tag to your fol-ol-lowers
vault_lines: I don't want no autograph
meaning:
Saba is communicating the idea that social media accounts with a large following have insincere interactions with their fans.

Before the age of social media, fans would (more often) request an autograph from a celebrity in person. Though the connection between celebrity and fan is temporary through this physical signing, it was nonetheless still a connection.

However, now in the digital age of social media, what is valued more is how many followers a particular celebrity has. A celebrity won’t “want no autograph” from any of their followers, and instead would want a “tag to [their] followers.”

line: Look, Solitaire more than a game with your card
vault_lines: Look, Solitaire more than a game with your card
meaning:
The objective of Solitaire is to create 4 piles of cards, with each pile belonging to the same suit (also displayed in ascending order, beginning with Ace to King). Notice the visual appearance of the cards.

Firstly, the game of Solitaire can be referred to as the game of social media: where the main goal is to achieve a certain visual appearance.

Secondly, take notice at how the colors and suits are separated into each piles. Perhaps this can represent the divide that social media can create between groups of individuals.

Finally, the order of the cards start with Ace card at the bottom, and with the King card on top. The card in interest is the King, given how it is displayed at the top of all the other cards. This may mean that social media users are just cards (“your card”), and that there’s a King card on top of all the other cards. A characteristic of social media is to have a particular individual (or card) on top/praised.

line: Internet turned me inanimate object

Saba points out that his insecurities are the reason why he feels the impulse to post on social media and because everyone holds the way he presents himself online in high regards, he has no other choice, but to play the same game and try to accurately present his true character through his social media.

Throughout the verse, Saba also seems to indirectly correlate the paranoia he feels due to the situation he Is in.

meaning:
Chance speaks – most likely from personal experience – about major labels signing rising icons to recording contracts.

Labels have been trying to sign him since his acclaimed Acid Rap mixtape dropped in 2013. To date, Chance has rather uniquely continued to reject their offers. He spoke on this in a recent interview with Fader magazine:

I’ve met with every A&R, VP of A&R, president of the labels, CEOs. I know all these people. I’ve had a lot of advice from people [in the industry] who wouldn’t give me that same advice today. It’s not even that they have any ill will towards me because I didn’t take their advice at the time. They’re almost like, ‘Keep going. You’re in uncharted territory, and you’re helping to shed light on what [the future of the business] will look like, and we’re all curious.’

Considering Chance as a bright firefly, record labels continue to pursue him in the hopes of catching him in a moment of personal/moral weakness (“when your lights go dim”) when he may give in to their offers. After signing to a label, they can take advantage of your celebrity status for self-promotion by making you part of their brand (“turn you to a letter in their logo”). Finally, after being locked into a contract artists often describe a loss of artistic freedom where labels only release material that conforms to their specifications (“stick you in a jar with a pen”).

When people start trying to take advantage of you in these ways, you know you’ve succeeded in becoming an icon.

So I hit up Jamie Foxx and was like, “Oh, I sampled the joint.” When he picked up the phone, he was on FaceTime with the camera facing the piano. Like, “I’m in the studio right now.” I’m like, “Damn, you know, this is ordained.” And I was like, “Yo, you know, I sampled a piece from I Might Need Security. Before I could finish my sentence, he started singing a new pass at “Fuck You.”

I was like, “Yo, this is gonna be tight.” But the end of the story, he never sent me anything. I didn’t get that shit before I put out the song. So, he’s not on it right now. But the point is, I brought in Peter because Peter knows how to take emotion or tone and make it a sound. And so, I gave him a little explanation of what it was and he took care of the hooks.

line: I donate to the schools next, they call me a deadbeat daddy The Sun-Times gettin’ that Rauner business

I just believe if we all believe in the government, even if we don’t necessarily believe it’s all the way fair, we all adhere to the government. We obey the law, pay taxes, and go through all the shit it takes to be a citizen. We should be able to rely on the government’s shit that they provide to us. So the first responders, parks, public hospitals, and obviously schools. That’s where kids go. Those are the people that we’re supposed to nurture, that are supposed to lead the next generation. Not all Chicago public schools are in terrible shape. It’s just how they fund them individually, what neighborhoods they’re in.

I went to Skinner, which is a really good school in Chicago, but it’s far from my house, far from where I grew up. If I went to my neighborhood school, Westcott—they were one of the schools that got like ten thousand dollars donated or something—I would’ve had a completely different education. And so I just thought that it would be important to at least bring awareness to school funding formulas on the state and district level, and just let people know that you got kids, that you might not be able to send your kids to private school, you know what I’m saying? You might not be able to send your kids to charter school. You’re supposed to be able to rely on your government to fully fund the shit that you pay for.

Yeah. So basically, a couple days after I donated some money to the schools, the front page of the Sun Times, which isn’t on a national level, but I live here. I walk on around, my family lives here. Everybody’s picked up these papers that say, “Spat Chance” on them. And it’s like a picture from me donating the money, but it’s basically an in-depth op-ed, opinion piece, which usually, you know, it’s like, “It’s on the front page?” About my child support. It wasn’t even really about my child support. The truth is, me and my daughter’s mother were trying to figure out a parenting schedule, not the child support. And they just pulled up all these legal documents that I think were public information, but made a whole piece about me that felt like it was just targeted. Maybe they were just doing their reporting. Maybe that is front page news; maybe that’s what was important for them. But I felt like I had just prodded somebody that had power on a government level, and a couple days later, there’s like a huge hit piece on every corner throughout the city.

The story came out and it was all truthful. They didn’t really throw any lies about me or anything, but I could tell that they were pissed about it. Luckily I live in a city where I feel like I have respect. I don’t have any real enemies or anything; it’s not like that. But it was just like, “Why the fuck would you do that?” You know? “Jay Elect” is a parallel leading  straight into “O' son of man” because by calling himself “Jay Elect,” Jay analogizes himself with Jesus Christ, who is “the Elect” (“the chosen one”) of God, as well as “the Son of Man” who is to do the will of God on earth. Christ called himself “the Son of Man” in the Bible.

Mark 14: 21, “For the Son of Man is to go just as it is written of Him; but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed!” (Source: The Bible)

And the terms “the Elect” and “Son of Man” both describe Christ in the The Book of Enoch, a non-canonical Jewish religious work:

Enoch 48:2: “In that hour was this Son of man invoked before the Lord of spirits, and his name in the presence of the Ancient of days…” And verse 5, “Therefore the Elect and the Concealed One existed in his presence, before the world was created, and for ever.”

Thus, just as Christ is the “Elect Son of Man” (God’s chosen man), so Jay sees himself as a person who is chosen by God to illuminate truth to the world.

“O' son of man” is also a reference to Revelation 10:5:

And the angel which I saw stand on the sea and on the earth lifted up his hand to heaven

In this verse, an angel comes down as the seventh trumpet blows and God answers all of life’s mysteries.

vault_lines: A fire in Cali'll swallow a valley for every African village burned
meaning:
Silicon Valley and the San Fernando Valley in California house some of the wealthiest people in the world.

Here, Jay implies that Californian forest fires are a result of atrocities that occur in Africa in the fight for materials (gold, previous stones, oil) to sell to the West.

One such example is the ruby field of Montepuez in Mozambique. According to Foreign Policy, 40% of the world’s rubies come from a mine run by Gemfields, a company that features the likes of Mila Kunis in their advertising campaigns.



In the same report, Foreign Policy documented that the Mozambique military burned down entire villages in 2014 in an attempt to force people to move away from the mine:

On Sept. 15, 2014, more than two years after Gemfields acquired rights to the concession through the joint venture with MRM, FIR operatives burned down some 300 houses in the market villages of Namucho and Ntoro, in the Namanhumbir region of Montepuez, and beat residents, according to interviews with the village chief, local residents, and artisanal miners.

This plays on the proverb “it takes a village to raise a child”; Chance feels that he was raised by his Chicago, and that they’re all a big family.

It’s part of Chicago culture that whenever someone makes it big, people often say “Oh him? Yea that’s my cousin!”—as a way of trying to “cosign” them. Now that Chance is a superstar, everyone in Chicago will try to cosign him.

It’s likely un-coincidental that this song features Chance’s cousin, Nicole.

line: The book don’t end with Malachi

meaning:
Malachi is the final book in the Hebrew Tanakh (the Old Testament) and the last minor prophet recorded in the Bible. Since Chance is a Christian, he believes in the New Testament which documents the life story and teachings of Jesus Christ.

There is a chronological gap of around 400 years between the OT and the NT, often known as the ‘period of silence’ between God and his people. The major Abrahamic religions disagree on the teachings of the NT. In doing so, Chance sets himself apart from the other ‘People of The Book’.

Interestingly, the opening lines of Malachi feature God boasting about his greatness, echoing the opening intro by Nicole and the choir.

You will see it with your own eyes and say, ‘Great is the Lord—even beyond the borders of Israel!’ (Malachi 1:5)

It also links with the previous line about spitting on Spotify. As a Christian, one has to spread the Good News and the teachings of Jesus Christ. As evidenced on this mixtape, Chance is integrating his personal belief into his music as his way of preaching.

Barak is the name or an old testament judge who defeated the Canaanites. The name means “lightning,” which correlates to the start of the next line with “electrify.”

While Jesus used the mustard seed metaphor simply to represent a very small amount of faith, Jay uses the term literally to describe a seed that he planted to cultivate a fruitful life for himself.

For many Christian denominations, specifically those that believe that the bread and wine offered at the altar transform into Jesus Christ’s true body and blood, the altar is a place to encounter God. This may also be referencing Psalms 43:4:

Then I will go to the altar of God,
to God, my joy and my delight.
I will praise you with the lyre,
O God, my God.

Interestingly, the next line refers to playing the lyre, a musical instrument, so this would be a fitting verse to interpolate into a song.

An altar is also used at a wedding (it’s the structure under which we commonly see the bride and groom affirm their love for one another and a priest pronounce them married). Justin could be talking about his rapid marriage to Hailey Baldwin; the two dated from 2015 to 2016, then reconciled in May of 2018 and got married within six months. He does this while also doing wordplay with a theme around magic. Parents often tell children that when they ask for something, they have to use the magic word: “please.” Here, Chance uses the word two times to emphasize his intent while also throwing the words “poof” and “Kadabra” (short for “Abracadabra”), which are often used by magicians at their shows.

In Chicago, single cigarettes are referred to as “looseys” or “loose squares.” “Wax” is a slang term for highly concentrated THC, which is the principal psychoactive constituent of cannabis. It’s the most fast and effective way to get high and, as certain weed usually does, makes its users lazy.

line: LA was the hideaway Lying in the jungle but you will not take my pride away
vault_lines: LA was the hideaway
meaning:
Chance plays with syllabic consonants in order to give these lines duality of meaning – they can be interpreted as both “Lying in the jungle…” or “Lion in the jungle…”  The second part of the second line builds on both meanings with more polysemic delivery.

Chance uses lions as a metaphor for his own family. The collective noun for a group of lions is a “pride” and lions are a savannah-dwelling mammal, despite the popular misconception that lions are “the king of the jungle”. In addition, lions are anthropomorphically characterized as regal, honorable and courageous – it is for this reason that they became known collectively as “prides” of lions; they were named after their associated characteristics, as many animal groups are.

Conversely, the line can be interpreted as “lying in the jungle”, which references Los Angeles' Baldwin Village – an area colloquially referred to as “The Jungle” due to its dense tropical foliage.

Chance also references The Lion King, Disney’s 1994 classic musical film – Simba, the protagonist of the film, is scared off into a jungle by his evil uncle, Scar, where he meets a warthog and a meerkat, Pumba and Timon who become his best friends and his foster-family. The jungle becomes a refuge for Simba, away from his home, Pride Rock, and his tyrannical uncle, paralleling how Chance feels about LA in comparison to Chicago.

Through synthesising both possible meanings, more wordplay can be realised. Lions are a part of the “big cat” family and spend a lot of their time resting – they spend time lying around. Furthermore, Simba grew up relaxing and living by the motto “Hakuna Matata” – “it means no worries for the rest of your days.”

line: No more knee slappin’ or shoe shinin’ or shoe signin’ ’Til the dream happens
vault_lines: No more knee slappin' or shoe shinin' or shoe signin'
meaning:
This line juxtaposes behavior that can stereotypically represent black servility–“knee slappin',” “shoe shinin',” and “shoe signin'”—to the larger process of change that these stereotypes can impede, specifically “the dream,” which references not only Martin Luther King’s “I Have a Dream” speech, but the legacy of creating actual equality for all in the United States.

“Knee slappin'” refers to low brow comedy of the minstrel-show type, comedy based upon reinforcing racist beliefs regarding African Americans, while “shoe-shinin'” is an occupation often stereotypically linked to African Americans. The professional athletic status necessary to perform “shoe signin'” may not seem of the same type as the previous two examples, but the use of “shoe signin'” as a close homophone for “shoe-shinin'” calls attention to the potential similarities between the two. Specifically, it indicates the way that professional athletes–and specifically black ones–are expected to perform non-threatening roles in in public settings. As recent public commentary around Colin Kaepernick’s political protests have made clear, many whites expect black athletes to stay in their places in ways that are akin to the stereotypical thoughts connected to minstrelsy and shoe shining–hence the significance of the third example in this line–in ways that limit progress towards equality.

Chance is sitting back, enjoying some weed, and tweeting, “I told you so,” at everyone who doubted him. Sipping on tea is a reference to a popular meme of Kermit the Frog drinking tea. Generally, the meme is set up with Kermit pointing out something detrimental, but instead of doing something to fix it, Kermit pettily sips tea while saying, “But that’s none of my business” instead.



The meme gained popularity after LeBron James posted an instagram picture where he wearing a hat with Kermit Sipping tea with the NBA Championship trophy after his Cleveland Cavaliers came back from a 3-1 series deficit to defeat the Golden State Warriors, a team which had set the regular-season win record that year.

In his opening lines, Chance explores astronomy, philosophy, and religion. Stars exist millions of light years away but appear from Earth to be a short distance away.



Stargazing often creates a sense of being mortal and insignificant in a cold, vast, ever-expanding universe. As Chance looks to the skies he is overwhelmed by the beauty and infinite size of space, which forces him into a kind of melancholy. He asks, where is God in all of this?

Connecting with the Creation story he references in the next line, Genesis 1:16 states:

Alternatively if the term stars is used to refer to celebrities, a deeper meaning is found. Chance describes them as inauthentic and indistinguishable from one another, saying they are both out of touch with people and God. line: Flint got clean water and y’all don’t got teen daughters And black friends and gay cousins, y’all just gon’ say nothin’

meaning:
While Chance can celebrate and enjoy his success, with his fans along for the ride, he reminds listeners of some harsh realities facing the US right now. These include misogyny, racism, and homophobia. He challenges listeners to not overlook the issues that plague a community in the same way we overcome every day issues in our personal lives. It’s a call for empathy.

He specifically references The Flint Water Crisis, which began in 2014 when the Flint River became the source of drinking water for the city of Flint, Michigan. Over 100,000 residents were exposed to high amounts of lead due to inadequate water treatment. It became a hot political talking point as commentators and residents argued over whether the city was being ignored for it being a “poor, black city”.



The issue was not resolved until early 2017, and even so it remains in process and reconstruction of pipelines probably won’t be completed until 2020.

meaning:
Record labels can restrict artists creatively by obliging them to release material suited to their wishes, potentially restricting which other artists they can collaborate with. Contractually, they own Chance’s friends.

Consider Chance’s longtime friend Vic Mensa who signed with Roc Nation in April 2015. Despite statements from Vic that his upcoming debut album, Traffic, would be released in 2015, it still hasn’t been given an official release date at the time this song was released. One thing we do know is that Chance is planned to be featured on it and hopes to secure another feature before it’s released.
