line: Slap-happy faggot slapper, bah-bah
vault_lines: Slap-happy faggot slapper, bah-bah
meaning:
“Faggot” is an insult traditionally aimed at gay men. This is one of Chance’s most controversial lines because he seems to be proud of homophobic violence.

In November 2013, Chance played a show at Middlebury College in Vermont. He was asked to censor this line because of the homophobic implications. After initially agreeing to the terms, he performed the song uncensored.

When asked about this line in an AMA, Chance expressed an awareness of and opposition to homophobia:


honestly, if a gay dude says nigga, i probably wouldnt even be that mad

gay dudes put up with a lot of hate, they honorary niggas


When Chance’s brother Taylor Bennett came out as bisexual, Chance publicly supported him.

Given this, it’s possible that Chance didn’t mean to be homophobic. “Faggot” is often used as a casual insult with little thought for its meaning. It’s also possible that he could have been playing on the two meanings of “gay” (happy and homosexual). Nonetheless, this lyric is careless at best, and has earned Chance criticism from Complex, Gawker, and lots of fans.

line: Asked Joseph about my deal He looked back said, “Hell yeah, let’s eat”

This line could be referring to either fellow rapper Joey Bada$$ or fellow Chicagoan and SAVEMONEY member Joey Purp.

“Eating” in hip-hop is a slang term for having success. At the time this record was released Chance was on the come up and was an independent artist, so when he asked either of them about a potential record deal he could sign, they supported him, encouraging him to have success.

However, Chance has remained independent after all that time and has found great success without any label backing him up.

This is also a reference to one of Chance’s favorite basketball teams, the Chicago Bulls. The lyric mentions 1992, the year the Bulls won their second of three consecutive championships, (3-peat). Likewise, Acid Rap is Chance’s second project and he’s planning on a 3-peat.

line: I feel like me and Taylor might still have sex Why?
vault_lines: I feel like me and Taylor might still have sex
meaning:
In 2009, Kanye made a scene at the VMAs when he rushed the stage and told Taylor Swift: “Yo Taylor, I’m really happy for you, I'mma let you finish, but Beyoncé had one of the best videos of all time.”

This prompted a huge media backlash against Kanye, and provoked public sympathy for Swift.

Swift’s first album after the controversy, Speak Now, sold 1.07 million copies first week—416,000 more than 2008’s Fearless. Whether this was due to Kanye’s influence is debatable, but numbers don’t lie: her popularity increase around 2010 is indisputable.

Kanye defended the line on Twitter, labelling “bitch” an endearing term and claiming he received Swift’s personal approval for the line. After a video showing Swift’s brother, Austin, trashing his Yeezy Boosts on Instagram went viral, Swift’s spokesperson released a statement claiming Kanye did not ask for approval, but rather for Swift to promote “Famous” on her Twitter feed, which she declined because of the “strong misogynistic message.” However, in an interview with ET Entertainment, Grammy Awards Producer Ken Ehrlich said: “She had an advance of [“Famous”], so she commented on it in a very funny way.”

Four days after the lyric was made public, Swift seemed to respond at the 58th Grammy Awards while receiving the Album of the Year award for 1989. She said:

There are going to be people along the way who will try to undercut your success, or take credit for your accomplishments or your fame, but if you just focus on the work and you don’t let those people sidetrack you, someday when you get where you’re going, you’ll look around and you will know that it was you and the people who love you who put you there, and that will be the greatest feeling in the world.

In leaked backstage SNL audio, Kanye labelled Swift a “fake ass.” On February 23, 2016, Kanye once again claimed he played Taylor the song and asked for her approval.

In an interview with GQ, Kim Kardashian corroborated ‘Ye’s claim that Swift “gave her blessings” for the line. On July 17, 2016, Kardashian posted videos to her Snapchat story which showed West and Swift talking about these lines over the phone:In August 2017, Taylor released her single “Look What You Made Me Do,“ which contains many references to the Kardashian West-Swift feud and the drama that came from "Famous.”

On March 20, 2020 a leaked video of the whole conversation between Swift and West about the line “I feel like me and Taylor might still have sex” hit the internet via Twitter and it revealed that the line was originally supposed to be “Taylor Swift might owe me sex.” This video also confirmed that Taylor’s version of the story behind the controversial line was true, since Kanye never mentioned the existence of the line “I made that bitch famous” in the video.

These lines draw similarities to that of Kanye’s verse on Jeezy’s “Put On,” which was released 8 years prior to “Famous,” and a year before the VMA stunt.

meaning:
Drapetomania was a fraudulent and racist theory proposed in 1851 by American physician Samuel A. Cartwright. He defined it as a mental illness that caused enslaved Black people to flee from captivity. The term comes from the Greek words drapetes (“a runaway slave”) and mania (“madness, frenzy”).
Cartwright’s theory was based on the false and self-serving belief that slavery was so beneficial to enslaved people that only a person suffering from a mental disorder would want to escape. He described the “symptoms” as including disobedience, insolence, and a refusal to work, and he even suggested “cures” like “whipping the devil out of them” as a preventative measure.
The concept of drapetomania has been thoroughly debunked as pseudoscience and is a clear example of “scientific racism,” which is the use of pseudo-scientific data and methods to justify racism. While Cartwright’s ideas were widely mocked in the North, they were reprinted and used to support the institution of slavery in the Southern United States.

Knowing that losing a castle can save the King, or trading a pawn can bring back the Queen is a knowledge only fools and genius' share.

[These lines remind me of my first day of kindergarten and, more generally, of the fear of being somewhere new.]

You have those moments all the time — your first day at your first job, or your [first] time going into the interview, your first time on stage, your first time having a baby. 1. Tempted by all the sins of the world and
2. Denied by the world.

Jesus invites us to follow him and follow his life. Sometimes we look at our lives and see that there is so much temptation and people around us telling us we are doing the wrong thing. Chance looks at Jesus’s life and sees that those things were happening to him. So even though it’s not fun, it’s to be expected if we are to follow God.

There is no better path to follow except the path of Jesus, so we can be sure that no matter our temptations and if the world tells us we are wrong: if we are following Jesus we can be sure that it’s the right path to be on.

line: Walkin’ through the desert, same mighty sword
vault_lines: Walkin’ through the desert, same mighty sword
meaning:
Apart from the sword imagery being an obvious metaphor for a rapper’s pen, this particular verse seems to reference to several biblical passages.

The Gospels of Matthew, Mark and Luke tell us that Jesus Himself wandered alone through the desert for 40 days, mirroring the Israelites journey from Egypt to the promised land of Canaan. In biblical narrative, the wilderness represents the process of sanctification – taken in its literal meaning, of being set apart for a specific purpose. The desert is a desolate, isolated space where God’s chosen ones are made holy, separated from the World and filled with God’s Spirit.

In Ephesians 6:10-20, the apostle Paul speaks of the “Armor of God”, of which God’s word represents “the sword of the Spirit”. Throughout the song, Chance tells us how he was left alone with nothing and no one other than himself and his pen – a metaphor for his lyrical ability. By referring to this same mighty “sword”, Chance could be nodding to Paul’s letter to the church of Ephesos, outlining a creative paralel between the word of God – a gift given unto humanity for its redemption – and his own talent for wordsmithing – a blessing given to him and the key to his own artistic redemption.

The specific phrasing “mighty sword”, however, is only found in Isaiah 27:1, a poem in which the prophet describes God’s reserved punishment for Leviathan (a great mythological sea serpent that symbolizes the enemies of God’s people), as well as the many blessings He has prepared for Israel. Chance might be alluding to this passage as a means of stating he always carried God’s promises of not only reparation, but an abundance of everlasting blessings.

line: Called out his arrogant lies, tossed him in a hole The middle of nowhere you never could find Where’s his money now? Where his wife at? Where his manager? Where his hype at? vault_lines: Where's his money now? Wherе his wife at?
meaning:
Chance the Rapper is known for his frequent biblical references, and in one section of his verse, he alludes to the figures of Daniel, Job, Moses, and Joseph in a concise manner.

The lines “Called out his arrogant lies, tossed him in a hole / The middle of nowhere you never could find” alludes to the story of Joseph, who was sold into slavery by his own family. Much like this track itself, the story of Joseph explores themes of abandonment, resilience and redemption.

As Genesis tells it, Joseph, a young man favored by his father, dreamt vivid dreams that spoke of a different future. These dreams, both a gift and a burden, created tension with his brothers, who accused the boy of lying about the prophecies that visited him in his sleep.

One day, Jacob sent his favorite son out to meet his brothers in Dothan, at a neighboring pasture where they tended to the family’s sheep. Driven by resentment, the young men conspired against him:

“They said to one another, ‘Here comes this dreamer. 20 Come now, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits. Then we will say that a fierce animal has devoured him, and we will see what will become of his dreams.’” (Genesis 37:19-20).
Joseph was then thrown into an empty pit, with no food or water, left to despair as his brothers debated whether or not to murder him – later settling for selling him as a slave to a traveling caravan.

Second, Chance addresses recent personal conflicts by questioning, “Where’s his money now? Where his wife at? Where his manager? Where his hype at?” This section of the verse also references the plight of Job, drawing parallels between Job’s trials and Chance’s own struggles, such as the public reaction to his last album, “The Big Day,” his divorce from Kirsten Corley after five years of marriage in 2024, and his legal dispute with former manager Pat Corcoran. Chance portrays a narrative akin to Job’s story, which serves as an exploration of suffering and faith.

Third, the line “Then they threw the dirt on the casket” symbolizes the end of a person’s life and ties Chance’s narrative to that of Job and Daniel, illustrating how their adversaries believed their downfall was inevitable.

Chance then transitions to the line “And into the hunt for the baby and the basket,” alluding to his survival despite attempts at his demise. This references the biblical story of Moses, who was placed in a basket and set adrift in the Nile River as a baby, ultimately leading to his rescue and redemption (Exodus 2:3-6).

Finally, in the line “Nobody Moses, alone with the mallet, That’s when the pen turned the stone to a tablet,” Chance draws parallels between himself and Moses regarding redemption. He suggests that like Moses, who etched the Ten Commandments into stone tablets alone on Mount Sinai in the presence of God, as Chance has taken a hiatus from the spotlight to refine his craft to regain his previous critical acclaim.

Order my steps in thy word and let not any iniquity have dominion over me.

In a callback to his verse on “Ultralight Beam,” Chance likens himself to the archangel Michael, ready to do God’s will and protect his family at any cost. Chance is a rapper—his gift are his words. Ephesian 6:17 states:

And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

God has given Chance his word, expressed with his lyricism and vocals, paralleling the next line saying God “gave Donnie a Trumpet.”

line: Jesus’ black life ain’t matter, I know, I talked to his daddy Said you the man of the house now, look out for your family
vault_lines: Jesus' black life ain't matter, I know, I talked to his daddy
meaning:
The historical Jesus was a Galilean Semite with olive-coloured skin. However, Christians around the world tend to imagine Jesus looking like them.  In America, that means that Jesus is often depicted as White. But Christians are supposed to believe that Jesus is with everyone and understands all our struggles – especially those who don’t have power during their Earthly existence.

The Black Lives Matter movement began in 2013, after the acquittal of George Zimmerman in the shooting death of Trayvon Martin. It aims to combat pervasive systematic racial injustice. Like many black people today, Jesus was killed by the authorities on flimsy grounds.  By saying “Jesus' black life ain’t matter,” Chance suggests that just like black lives are often casualties of the American racist society, Jesus Christ was a casualty of the racist and imperial Roman/Hebrew society.

In 2015, Chance became a father. God has tasked him to look after his daughter and her mother, which has given him a real sense of responsibility.

line: I don’t make songs for free, I make ’em for freedom Don’t believe in kings, believe in the Kingdom
vault_lines: I don't make songs for free, I make 'em for freedom
meaning:
Chance’s approach of releasing his music for free serves a bigger purpose than just to keep creative control over it.

As Chance said in his verified annotation from Kanye West’s “Ultralight Beam,” he sees himself as the “Tubman of the underground,” one who is able to lead other artists to their independence from record labels.



This is why he doesn’t believe in people who rule over others' decisions (record labels a.k.a kings), but rather in the ones who actually care about their craft and want to build their own path (artists a.k.a the kingdom).

This could also have an alternate meaning, as Chance could be talking about how people shouldn’t believe in kings from Earth, but rather believe in the Kingdom of God.

line: I’m at war with my wrongs, I’m writing four different songs I never forged it or forfeited, I’m a force to be reconciled They want four-minute songs You need a four-hour praise dance performed every morn
vault_lines: I'm at war with my wrongs, I'm writing four different songs
meaning:
Reminiscent of Kanye’s desire, Chance wants to right his wrongs. In order to do it, he’s started to praise God by making his writing style more gospel-focused. Since then, Chance has come out with songs like “Sunday Candy,” “Angels,” “Somewhere In Paradise,” and a well-regarded feature on Kanye West’s “Ultralight Beam.” Chance’s clearly devoted to make this his mission, as he feels that one individual song isn’t enough to praise God’s name.

The line “I never forged it or forfeited” means that Chance never faked or quit on his quest to reach where he’s at now. The line “I’m a force to be reconciled” is a play on the phrase “a force to be reckoned with.” Chance states that he’s not making music to see other rappers fall, but rather to push hip-hop into new horizons and see them at the top with him.

Finally, Chance’s use of alliterations becomes evident, as he plays with the homophones “four” and “for”:

I’m at war with my wrongs, I’m writing four different songs
I never forged it or forfeited, I’m a force to be reconciled
They want four minute songs
You need a four hour praise dance performed every morn

The constant use of the number four in this song is yet another reference to Christianity as it’s a symbolic number in the religion as a whole—four gospels/evangelists, the four marks of the Church, etc. This is without mentioning that Chance does this in four lines of this verse.

line: And gave Donnie a trumpet in case I get shortness of breath
vault_lines: And gave Donnie a trumpet in case I get shortness of breath
meaning:
Chance has been friends with Nico Segal, previously known as Donnie Trumpet, since childhood. Segal plays trumpet in The Social Experiment.

Trumpets have symbolic resonance in the Bible. Most importantly, it is said that a trumpet will sound at the end of the world, and raise the dead into new life. Although God gave Chance his voice as a gift, He also gave Nico the ability to play the trumpet. If Chance dies, Nico’s trumpet will bring him back.



This line comes at the end of the verse (when Chano may be actually running out of breath) and a trumpet can be heard in the instrumental.




A few days after this song premiered, Chance had to cancel a performance in NYC due to being hospitalized for pneumonia. Ironically, one of the most common symptoms of pneumonia is shortness of breath.

line: I’m feeling shortness of breath, so Nico grab you a horn Hit Jericho with a buzzer beater to end a quarter Watch brick and mortar fall like dripping water, ugh (Good God)
vault_lines: I'm feeling shortness of breath, so Nico grab you a horn
meaning:
Playing with the last line of the first verse while mentioning his friend Nico for the second time, Chance alludes to Joshua 6, which tells the story of the Battle of Jericho.

The Walls of Jericho protected the land of Canaan from the Israelites. In the battle, the Israelites circled the walls once per day for the first six days, then circled the walls seven times on the final day. Under Joshua’s command, the Israelites blew trumpets made out of ram’s horns to knock the walls down. It’s no coincidence Nico’s trumpet is played throughout the song.



Byron uses the walls of Jericho to describe the struggles one encounters in life. Similar to how Israelites’s faith was strong enough to break the walls down, if you work hard enough and have faith in yourself and The Lord, then everything will become possible.

line: They booked the nicest hotels on the 59th floor With the big wide windows, with the suicide doors
vault_lines: They booked the nicest hotels on the 59th floor
meaning:
“Suicide doors” are car doors designed to open on an opposite hinge than regular doors. They can be regularly found in luxury cars.



Chance plays with the term, pointing out that a life which revolves around materialism will kill your soul. People let their material possessions own them, to the point where they can’t live without them anymore, losing themselves in the process. This is reminiscent of Kanye’s line on “All Falls Down”:

It seems we living the American dream
But the people highest up got the lowest self-esteem

This also points to the value of privacy for himself and his family—in “Ultralight Beam” he rapped: “My daughter look just like Sia you can’t see her.” Wide windows is a nod to over exposure—they make someone vulnerable and visible which could lead to suicide.

line: Dying laughing with Krillin saying something ’bout blonde hair
vault_lines: Dying laughing with Krillin saying something 'bout blonde hair
meaning:
Krillin is a character from the manga/anime series Dragon Ball Z.

“Saying something ‘bout blonde hair” is a reference to Krillin’s friend Goku, who achieves a new level of power called Super Saiyan after he witnesses Krillin’s death. Super Saiyans have incredible strength and Goku’s hair changes from black to blonde. “Saying” is also a play on the word “Saiyan”. Krillin’s wife, Android 18, also had blonde hair, another of the blessings in his life. Krillin’s death could also tie into the previous line of “whistle me into song air,” since he was killed by Frieza by being sent flying into the atmosphere until he exploded.

This line also connects with the next one as Chance is laughing at the fact that Jesus is often portrayed as a white man when he was actually a Galilean Jew with olive-coloured skin.



There is also an ongoing joke amongst DBZ fans that Krillin is an underpowered character and is always dying/getting owned, hence why Chance is “dying laughing” with him.

This isn’t the first time Chance has referenced the popular anime series. He has tweeted about characters and also referenced another Saiyan power on Mick Jenkins' song “Crossroads.”

line: I know the difference in blessings and worldly possessions Like my ex-girl getting pregnant And her becoming my everything
vault_lines: I know the difference in blessings and worldly possessions
meaning:
In a culture where material items like money are considered blessings, Chance uses his daughter as an example of what a true blessing is. While getting his ex girl pregnant was not initially a blessing, it became one when his daughter was born. In addition to this, worldy possession are tied to the Earth and will remain there even if you pass away. Blessings on the other hand, are not held or tied down, they instead fall as mercy from God’s kingdom.

The message is similar to the one in Matthew 6:19-21:

Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal. But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal. For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.

line: I’m gon’ praise Him, praise Him ’til I’m gone I’m gon’ praise Him, praise Him ’til I’m gone When the praises go up, the blessings come down When the praises go up, the blessings come down It seems like blessings keep falling in my lap It seems like blessings keep falling in my lap
vault_lines: I'm gon' praise Him, praise Him 'til I'm gone
meaning:
Praying is a reinforcement and profession of faith. See 1 Chronicles 16:9:

Sing to Him, sing praises to Him; speak of all His wonders

Chance believes he’s reaping the rewards that come from loving and praising God. Among the rewards are the birth of his first daughter, Kensli, and his success as an artist. He alluded to the latter on “Ultralight Beam.”

The “praises go up/blessings come down” bit is inspired by the classic Sunday school song “The Wise Man and the Foolish Man”. The melodies in both songs oscillate with the lyrics.

The final hook includes an interpolation of Fred Hammond’s “Let the Praise Begin.” This reiterates the message of the song. Blessings and miracles are coming when you least expect them, similar to how Chance wasn’t expecting to have a daughter.

“Daddy used to work that Streets and San” is a reference to the City of Chicago’s Department of Streets and Sanitation where Chance’s father, Ken Williams-Bennett, worked when Chance and his brother were kids.

This ties is to a lyric from the song “Summer Friends” on Coloring Book:

Dad was working late, he treat the crib like it’s a timeshare.

The fellow Chicagoan then went on to work for Barack Obama when he was a U.S. Senator from Illinois and, eventually, to the seat of the president. Chance’s father has an extensive background in politics and used to work hard to provide for his family while being able to make a difference in Chicago. Chance admires his father’s work ethic and credits him for playing a part in the election of the first African-American president.

meaning:
Many biblical authors acknowledge God as their protector, or one who shields them from harm. Take an example from Ephesians 6:16:

Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked.

In a popular instance of biblical imagery, The Apostle Paul refers to the power of faith in God to deflect attacks from the enemy.

Here, Chance refers to this imagery to illustrate a more modern take on this verse, whereas Chance is protected by a force field through which nothing can penetrate, keeping him completely protected. Paul uses flaming arrows against a shield, Chance uses shots against a force field.

By referring to himself as “a force in the field,” Chance is also referencing his dedication to making a difference in his community through philanthropy and sharing the Gospel. Chance is known for personally making efforts to improve conditions in his home-city, such as through donations to public schools in Chicago.

line: This is the beat that played under the Word This is the sheep that ain’t like what it heard
vault_lines: This is like this many rings
meaning:
Note Chance’s use of the homophones herd and heard. In popular culture, a sheep is a person who doesn’t think for themselves and only follows others (the herd). This relates to how many artists sign with a label thinking that it’s the only way to be recognized in the industry since the artists before them also did the same.

Chance is the exception to that rule. He didn’t like what he heard from others—case in point:

Labels told me to my face that they own my friends

Therefore, Chance decided early on not to follow the status quo and instead go in his own direction to prove to everyone that he can be as successful as any other artist, without a label to back him up.

Also note that the sheep is a symbolic reference for sacrifice and its symbolism occurs frequently within the bible.

line: This is officially first
vault_lines: This is officially first
meaning:
Coloring Book was Chance’s first commercially released project. His two previous mixtapes, 10 Day and Acid Rap, were only released as free downloads, whereas Coloring Book is available through subscription streaming services.

Many organisations don’t consider a project to be eligible for awards unless it is commercially released. It wasn’t until after this song was released that the Recording Academy allowed non-commercial releases to be eligible for Grammy awards.

Chance isn’t shy about his opinions on this topic, referring it on Kanye West’s “Ultralight Beam” and even signing a Change.org petition that demanded The Grammys to consider free projects in their eligibility.



Complex even listed Acid Rap as one of the mixtapes that most deserved a Grammy, but couldn’t because of regulations, saying:

The day Acid Rap came out was the first time the Chicago hip-hop website Fake Shore Drive had crashed since the G.O.O.D. Music “Don’t Like” remix dropped. And it’s a safe bet that all the people who had been awaiting it, whether they made a successful trip to Chicago’s premier hip-hop blog or grabbed the first link from whichever obscure file hosting site they found, once they got it, they were stuck on it for the rest of the day.

Coloring Book and “No Problem” both won Grammys in 2017.

meaning:
In the biblical story of Adam and Eve, the serpent tempts Eve to eat from the tree of knowledge of good and evil. This breaks the only rule God had set for them, and gets them kicked out of the Garden of Eden.

Sometimes the serpent is seen as personifying the Devil, but the story doesn’t support this—it’s better to think of it as a physical representation of temptation. Chance follows God’s path, as preached in sermons, and does not succumb to temptation. In fact, not only does Chance not succumb to temptation, he doesn’t even allow himself to come into a place where he is liable to be tempted. He won’t even talk to the serpent.

Discernment, in Christian contexts, is the ability to tell right from wrong in everyday life. Chance is trying to do the right thing in every area of his life.

line: Fall quarter was just a tall order

meaning:
A “tall order” is a big challenge or difficult task. Getting through autumn or “fall” was a struggle for Chance since his “big homie” Rod was killed around September 2011.

Chance plays off the season “fall” with the “fall” (trip down from drugs) mentioned in the previous line. He’s literally doing drugs just to make the time go by faster or to get through it.

line: As of late, all my verses seem not so verse-y And all my words just mean controversy
vault_lines: As of late, all my verses seem not so verse-y

line: My big homie died young, just turned older than him I seen it happen, I seen it happen, I see it always He still be screaming, I see his demons in empty hallways
vault_lines: My big homie died young, just turned older than him
meaning:
These lines are about Chance’s friend, Rodney Kyles Jr., who was stabbed at Lincoln Park, Chicago. He was only 19 years old when he died, Chance was 18 at the time and now he has surpassed that age.

This murder had a profound effect on a young Chance and he is haunted by the image of his friend’s final moments as he died. In an interview with the Chicago Reader, Chance spoke about the incident saying that he was there when Rodney was stabbed:

It was a really big thing because I was there and I saw it and I was really affected by it on a very personal level

By saying that he ‘sees it always’, he is commenting on the high murder rate in his hometown, which means that Rodney’s case is often repeated. This also means that Chance has repeated nightmares or flashbacks of Rod’s brutal murder.



Chance spoke at length about this incident when Sway asked him specifically about these lyrics.

line: Before I believed in not believing in

meaning:
Ignorance is bliss. There was a time when Chance believed in things. Since he references Jesus in the last line, “not believing in” might be a reference to Atheism or simply just not believing what the masses believe about any subject.

Just before this, Chance mentioned a time when MJ was in the height of his success. Later MJ’s image was stained by his alleged child molestation charges. Chance uses this line to reflect on the innocence of his childhood, a time when he didn’t believe the negativity surrounding his heroes. However, he has now matured and witnessed first hand the evil that exists in the world around him.

line: Sometimes the truth don’t rhyme Sometime the lies get millions of views

Referring to the previous line, “foams” doesn’t rhyme with “picked,” nor “sick,” nor “rich.” Chance just said it because it’s the pure and cold truth about the times we live in.

Chance is also letting us know that, just like he did with the previous line, the truth won’t always “rhyme” or sound pretty and it will be the hardest thing to hear sometimes. Meanwhile, a lie will always be more appealing and therefore it’ll be the one people will accept more because they’ll rather stay ignorant than face the facts and make a change.

line: Wore my feelings on my sleeveless
vault_lines: Wore my feelings on my sleeveless
meaning:
The classic saying from Othello is “wear your heart on your sleeve”, which means that your feelings are for everyone to see.

Through his raps, Chance is letting everyone see how he feels; Acid Rap is a very personal mixtape. Since he’s wearing a sleeveless shirt, it makes his feelings more real and even more exposed because they would be around his bear arms rather than on the sleeve of a shirt.

An alternate explanation, however, could be that it’s a play on the word sleeveless (sleeve-less) meaning that Chance has learned to not be as emotional or get his feelings hurt because he wears his feelings on his sleeve less often.

line: Stressin’, pullin’ my hair out, hoping I don’t get picked
vault_lines: Stressin', pullin' my hair out, hoping I don't get picked
meaning:
This is a quadruple entendre focused on the word “picked”, meaning that there are four meanings to this line:


A reference to a hair pick or afro comb, a tool used to shape curly or afro hair which has a lot of history and is usually worn by people with afros.
Getting “picked” is another way of referring to being robbed.
Getting “picked” for a sports team, which plays off of the previous bar (“took the team up off my back”).
Chance doesn’t want to die any time sooner due to the extensive gun violence in the streets of Chicago. He metaphorically hopes he’s not the next to be picked to die by God.

Chance’s hungry for success, but he’s not going to sacrifice his quality or ideals to get there. He’s analytical and makes the best decisions for himself at the right time.

In 2017, Chano’s dream of playing arenas came true when he embarked on the “Be Encouraged Tour,” an extensive arena tour throughout the United States.

As a famous rapper once rapped: “Mo' Money, Mo' Problems.”

line: Mom still thinks I should go back to school

line: For future hoopers dead from Rugers Shooting through the empty alley Could’ve threw him an alley-oop Helping him do good in school

meaning:
Rugers is gun brand. An “alley-oop” is a collaborative play in basketball in which one player throws the ball near the basket to a teammate who jumps, catches the ball in mid air and puts it in the hoop.

Chance plays with the word “shooting” to paint a dark image about how kids with huge potential get killed in the streets for no good reason at all. In connection with the previous line, Chance could be saying that instead of using children to kill each other, the gangs could provide a place where they can help them achieve their dreams with the influence and numbers they have in the city. “Helping him do good in school” could also refer to alley-oop.com, a math tutoring website which was live at the time of the song’s release.

This could most likely be a reference to Tyrone Lawson, a Chicago teen, and the January 2013 incident where the young basketball player was shot and killed after the game. A similar death occurred back in 1984 when Ben Wilson, the top basketball recruit in the country at the time, was gunned down.



A picture of Tyrone Lawson

line: Damn that acid burn when it clean ya
vault_lines: Damn that acid burn when it clean ya
meaning:
Chance is hitting us with a double entendre here. In science, an acid is any chemical compound that, when dissolved in water, gives a solution with a pH less than 7.0. They tend to be present in cleaning solutions designed to cut through difficult grease and stains. However, if you get some of it in your eyes or under your skin, it burns like no tomorrow.

Meanwhile, psychedelics, such as acid, can make the user highly introspective. Chance’s talking about the pain of seeing one’s life for what it is while at the same time the cleansing and cathartic effect that it has to face one’s problems head on. It is said to either make you a better person, or completely destroy you.

Additionally, those familiar with a variety of psychedelics will note that synthetic psychedelics like acid, (or research chemicals that are often sold as “acid,” etc.), can leave a clean-burning feeling for hours after the comedown, unlike mushrooms.

line: Every time they buy a verse, I buy a purse But you can’t buy back time, that’s just not how it works

Even though I didn’t have a job, my girl was working three jobs when she was with me and providing me a place to stay and food to eat and everything.

 When I first got money I was very selfish about my money. In more recent times I’ve grown to be accepting of getting rid of the thought of my woman ever wanting me for my money or wanting me for any type of success that I got and start to be able to share with her the things that she helped me get. Even with that, that’s not how you pay it back. That’s not equivalent, by any means, to the actual time and work that she put in to building my family.

That’s why there are so many kids' parents that are like, “You better go to college.” Like, “Your ass didn’t go to college.”

The whole song is just about creating a home, creating a space that is ours, that’s locked down. That for our daughter and our kids-to-be’s for their growth. That whole line is just about us getting past all the shit that we had to do that we’ve put each other through and creating a space for our lineage to grow.

line: We hit the Shell station, I tell you stay in the car

And I’m also not finna… I tell her, “Don’t turn off the car, don’t park that joint.”  That’s a thing I think a lot of people could relate to, from Chicago, just knowing how we move most of the time. The gas station—its fucked up shit that happens at the gas station.

My homie died last year at a fuckin' gas station. I think that was always how we moved. And what’s funny is like, I move that way ‘cause I was from out South. My girl lived on the North side for a lot of her life. She grew up in Hyde Park, but iher sister had the foresight to invest black, in the neighborhood. We had to live there in the beginning 'cause that’s where we was living. That’s how long she’s been riding with me. Obviously after hearing it a million times, she didn’t want to hear that shit no more. But if she was to ask me to play a song, it was the most validation that I could feel out of anybody saying anything about my music. So yeah, where’s the return on investment?
